title: Composite Appeal Maintainable Where Common Judgment Decides Two Connected Suits By Same Plaintiff: Supreme Court
judge: Justice Vikram Nath & Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah
subject: Civil Law

summary.background: The appellant filed two connected civil suits for declaration of title and perpetual injunction against the respondents. Both suits involved identical properties and overlapping parties. The Trial Court consolidated the proceedings and disposed of both suits via a single common judgment.
summary.issues: Whether a single composite appeal filed under Order 41 Rule 1 CPC against a common judgment deciding two connected civil suits is legally maintainable without filing two separate memorandum of appeals.
summary.relevantLaw: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — Order 41 Rule 1 & Section 11 (Res Judicata).
summary.courtReasoning: The Supreme Court observed that where two suits between the same parties involving identical issues are tried together and decided by a common judgment, insisting on separate technical appeals places an unnecessary procedural burden on litigants. Since the findings in both suits were identical and consolidated, a single composite appeal with certified copy of the common judgment satisfies statutory mandates.
summary.holding: A single composite appeal challenging a common decree arising from consolidated trial court suits is legally maintainable.
summary.keyPrinciple: Procedural rules under Order 41 CPC are handmaids of justice and should not defeat substantive appellate rights when a single decree is impugned.
summary.outcome: Appeal allowed; High Court order dismissing the composite appeal set aside; appeal restored on merits.

title: Section 42 NDPS Act: Substantial Compliance Sufficient Where Urgent Search Risk Removing Contraband: Supreme Court
judge: Justice J.B. Pardiwala & Justice K. Vinod Chandran
subject: Criminal Law
actsInvolved: Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985

summary.background: Police officers received secret information during night patrolling regarding illicit narcotics transportation in a commercial vehicle. The officers executed an immediate search without waiting to record grounds of belief in writing prior to search, citing risk of removal.
summary.issues: Whether total literal recording prior to search under Section 42(1) NDPS Act is mandatory even when immediate search is necessary to prevent concealment or escape of offender.
summary.courtReasoning: The Court held that while Section 42 contains safeguards against arbitrary search, total compliance cannot mean impeding urgent enforcement where delay allows contraband to vanish. Substantial compliance recorded immediately after seizure fulfills statutory intent.
summary.holding: Immediate search without prior written entry is valid if recorded forthwith post-operation with recorded reasons for emergency.
summary.keyPrinciple: Emergency exceptions in Section 42 NDPS Act protect bona fide enforcement where immediate action prevents destruction of drug evidence.
summary.outcome: High Court acquittal set aside; conviction under Section 21 NDPS Act restored.

title: Wife and Children Entitled to Consortium: Supreme Court Enhances Motor Accident Compensation to Rs 12.47 Lakh
judge: Justice Surya Kant & Justice Dipankar Datta
subject: Motor Accident Law

summary.background: The victim died in a fatal road accident involving a heavy transport vehicle. The Motor Accident Claims Tribunal awarded compensation of Rs 6.8 Lakhs, which the High Court slightly enhanced. The dependents appealed seeking full spousal, parental, and filial consortium.
summary.issues: Whether each surviving dependent (widow and children) is independently entitled to consortium heads under Motor Vehicles Act compensation standards established in Pranay Sethi and Magma General Insurance.
summary.courtReasoning: The Supreme Court affirmed that consortium is not limited to a single lump-sum for the family. Each child is entitled to parental consortium of Rs 40,000 (plus 10% enhancement), and the widow is entitled to spousal consortium.
summary.holding: Spousal, parental, and filial consortium must be awarded individually to all eligible legal representatives.
summary.keyPrinciple: Comprehensive loss of companionship under MV Act must be calculated per dependent rather than per household.
summary.outcome: Compensation enhanced from Rs 7.2 Lakhs to Rs 12.47 Lakhs with 7.5% interest per annum.

title: Residential House Exemption U/S 60(1)(ccc) CPC Is Personal to Judgment-Debtor, Cannot Be Claimed by Legal Heirs: Supreme Court
judge: Justice Abhay S. Oka & Justice Ujjal Bhuyan
subject: Civil Law

summary.background: Bank obtained a money decree against original judgment-debtor. During execution proceedings, the original debtor passed away. His legal heirs resisted attachment of the single residential house claiming statutory immunity under Section 60(1)(ccc) CPC.
summary.issues: Whether the statutory protection against attachment of a main residential house under Section 60(1)(ccc) CPC is a personal privilege of the living debtor or an inheritable immunity by legal heirs.
summary.relevantLaw: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 — Section 60(1)(ccc) & Section 50 (Liability of Legal Representatives).
summary.courtReasoning: The Court held that the legislative object of Section 60(1)(ccc) is to prevent homelessness of an living judgment-debtor during his lifetime. Upon death, the estate devolves on legal representatives under Section 50 CPC, who inherit property subject to decree liabilities.
summary.holding: Statutory exemption under Section 60(1)(ccc) CPC is personal to the judgment-debtor and lapses upon his death.
summary.keyPrinciple: Statutory execution exemptions designed for personal protection do not insulate inherited property from ancestral decree satisfaction.
summary.outcome: Appeal dismissed; bank permitted to proceed with execution of decree against inherited residential property.

title: Advocates Acting as Insolvency Professionals Liable to Pay GST Under Forward Charge: Delhi High Court
respondent: Union of India & Central Board of Indirect Taxes
judge: Justice Yashwant Varma & Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav
subject: Tax Law
actsInvolved: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017

summary.background: Petitioners challenged tax notices levying GST on fees earned by enrolled advocates while functioning as Resolution Professionals or Liquidators under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.
summary.issues: Whether legal representation exemption and reverse charge mechanism under GST applies when an advocate acts in the statutory capacity of an Insolvency Professional.
summary.relevantLaw: CGST Act 2017 — Section 9(3) Notification No. 13/2017 & IBC 2016.
summary.courtReasoning: The High Court held that reverse charge protection applies strictly to legal services provided by an advocate qua advocate. When an advocate acts as Resolution Professional, they perform statutory administrative functions under IBC, distinct from legal advocacy.
summary.holding: Services rendered as Resolution Professional / Liquidator are taxable under forward charge and do not enjoy advocate legal service exemption.
summary.keyPrinciple: Tax exemptions attach to the specific statutory nature of services provided rather than the professional qualification of the individual.
summary.outcome: Writ petition disposed of with clarification on forward charge applicability.

title: Reporting Official Arrest Without Defamatory Intent Cannot Attract Criminal Prosecution: Kerala High Court
subject: Constitutional Law

summary.background: A newspaper published news reporting the arrest of a public official by vigilance police based on official press releases. The official filed criminal defamation proceedings claiming injury to reputation.
summary.issues: Whether accurate journalistic reporting of official law enforcement actions constitutes criminal defamation under Section 499 IPC.
summary.courtReasoning: The High Court observed that reporting official police arrests conducted in public discharge of duty falls under public interest exceptions. Criminal defamation cannot be used to intimidate journalists reporting true facts sourced from law enforcement agencies.
summary.holding: Accurate reporting of police actions without malice is protected under Exception 4 of Section 499 IPC.
summary.keyPrinciple: Freedom of press encompasses reporting verified official actions without fear of criminal prosecution.
summary.outcome: Criminal defamation complaint against journalists quashed.

title: Section 34 Arbitration Act: Court Cannot Modify Arbitral Award, Can Only Confirm or Set Aside: Supreme Court Bench
judge: Justice R.F. Nariman & Justice B.R. Gavai
subject: Arbitration Law

summary.background: District Court in Section 34 proceedings modified the compensation rate awarded by the Arbitrator in land acquisition arbitration. High Court upheld the modification under appellate jurisdiction.
summary.issues: Whether Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996 empowers courts to vary or modify arbitral awards or merely permits setting aside.
summary.relevantLaw: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 — Section 34 & UNCITRAL Model Law Article 34.
summary.courtReasoning: The Supreme Court emphasized that Section 34 is modeled on UNCITRAL Model Law which deliberately avoids conferring power to modify awards. Minimal judicial intervention is the cornerstone of arbitration law. If an award is patently illegal, the court must set it aside and relegate parties to fresh proceedings.
summary.holding: Courts exercising Section 34 jurisdiction cannot modify, rewrite, or alter arbitral awards.
summary.keyPrinciple: Judicial review under Section 34 is supervisory, not appellate; courts can set aside awards but cannot rewrite arbitrator findings.
summary.outcome: Appeal allowed; judicial modification of award set aside.

title: Daughters Have Equal Coparcenary Rights By Birth Under 2005 Amendment Unaffected By Date of Father's Death: Supreme Court
judge: Justice Arun Mishra & Justice S. Abdul Nazeer & Justice M.R. Shah
subject: Family Law

summary.background: Daughter filed partition suit claiming 1/3rd equal share in ancestral coparcenary property. Brothers contested alleging that father died prior to September 9, 2005 amendment, rendering daughter ineligible.
summary.issues: Whether statutory coparcenary status conferred upon daughters under Section 6 Hindu Succession Act requires the coparcener father to be alive on September 9, 2005.
summary.relevantLaw: Hindu Succession Act 1956 — Section 6 as amended in 2005.
summary.courtReasoning: Reaffirming Vineeta Sharma principles, the Court held that coparcenary status is acquired by birth. It is an unobstructed heritage. The death of the father prior to 2005 does not divest the daughter's right conferred by statutory birthright.
summary.holding: Daughters possess equal coparcenary rights by birth in ancestral property regardless of whether father was alive on Sept 9, 2005.
summary.keyPrinciple: Section 6 HSA 2005 amendment operates retroactively to grant equal status to daughters from birth.
summary.outcome: Partition decree modified to award daughter equal coparcenary share.

title: Zero FIR Registration Mandatory Under Section 173 BNSS: Supreme Court Guidelines on Police Jurisdiction
judge: Justice D.Y. Chandrachud & Justice P.S. Narasimha
subject: Criminal Law

summary.background: Victim attempted to lodge complaint of grave cognizable offence at police station where offence did not occur. Police refused registration citing territorial jurisdiction limits.
summary.issues: Whether police officers are bound to register Zero FIR immediately upon receiving cognizable offence information regardless of territorial limits.
summary.relevantLaw: BNSS 2023 Section 173 & Lalita Kumari v. Govt of UP precedent.
summary.courtReasoning: The Court mandated that territorial jurisdiction is irrelevant at the stage of FIR registration. Police must register Zero FIR, initiate emergency medical/forensic preservation, and subsequently transfer case files to jurisdictional station.
summary.holding: Registration of Zero FIR is mandatory upon receipt of cognizable offence disclosure.
summary.keyPrinciple: Procedural boundaries cannot delay crime reporting or victim access to criminal justice.
summary.outcome: Guidelines issued to all Director Generals of Police across States & Union Territories.

title: Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma: Daughters Have Equal Coparcenary Rights By Birth Under Section 6 Hindu Succession Act
judge: Justice Arun Mishra, Justice S. Abdul Nazeer & Justice M.R. Shah
subject: Personal Law

summary.background: Conflicting Supreme Court decisions (Prakash v. Phulavati & Danamma v. Amar) existed on whether a daughter's coparcenary right under amended Section 6 HSA depends on her father being alive on 09.09.2005.
summary.issues: Whether the 2005 Amendment to Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act confers coparcenary status on daughters by birth regardless of whether father was living on amendment date.
summary.relevantLaw: Hindu Succession Act, 1956 — Section 6 (as amended by Act 39 of 2005).
summary.courtReasoning: The 3-Judge Bench held that coparcenary right is conferred by birth. It is an unobstructed heritage. The status of living father on 09.09.2005 is irrelevant. The statutory right attached from birth.
summary.holding: Daughters are coparceners by birth with equal rights and liabilities as sons in Joint Hindu Family property.
summary.keyPrinciple: Coparcenary right of a Hindu daughter is created by birth under Section 6 HSA and does not depend on living status of father on 2005 amendment date.
summary.outcome: Reference answered; Prakash v. Phulavati overruled; coparcenary rights of daughters fully protected.

title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala: Basic Structure Doctrine of the Indian Constitution
judge: Chief Justice S.M. Sikri & 12 Other Judges
subject: Constitutional Law

summary.background: Challenge to the 24th, 25th, and 29th Constitutional Amendments which sought to limit fundamental rights and grant unlimited amending power to Parliament under Article 368.
summary.issues: What is the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution of India under Article 368?
summary.relevantLaw: Constitution of India — Article 368, Article 13 & Part III Fundamental Rights.
summary.courtReasoning: By a 7:6 majority, the 13-Judge Bench established that while Parliament has broad power to amend any part of the Constitution including fundamental rights, it cannot alter, damage or destroy the essential features or 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.
summary.holding: Article 368 does not enable Parliament to alter the basic structure or framework of the Constitution.
summary.keyPrinciple: Parliamentary amending power under Article 368 is limited and cannot abrogate basic structure pillars like judicial review, rule of law, and secularism.
summary.outcome: Basic Structure Doctrine established as fundamental constitutional law of India.

title: Residential House Exemption U/S 60(1)(ccc) CPC Is Personal to Judgment-Debtor, Cannot Be Claimed by Legal Representatives: Supreme Court
judge: Justice P.S. Narasimha & Justice Alok Aradhe
subject: Civil Law

summary.background: Bank sought execution of money decree by attaching the residential house of deceased borrower. The legal representatives claimed statutory exemption under Section 60(1)(ccc) CPC as applicable in Punjab & Haryana.
summary.issues: Whether statutory exemption against attachment of a sole residential house under Section 60(1)(ccc) CPC survives the death of the judgment-debtor for benefit of legal heirs.
summary.courtReasoning: The Supreme Court analyzed the statutory text and held that the protection is personal to the judgment-debtor to prevent destitution during their lifetime. It does not create an inheritable immunity for legal representatives who inherit the estate subject to debts.
summary.holding: Section 60(1)(ccc) CPC exemption is strictly personal to the judgment-debtor and cannot be invoked by legal heirs after death.
summary.keyPrinciple: Statutory execution exemptions designed for personal protection do not insulate inherited property from ancestral decree satisfaction.
summary.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Bank permitted to proceed with execution auction.

title: Arbitration Clause in Unstamped Agreement Enforceable For Seeking Interim Measures: Supreme Court
judge: Justice Dr. D.Y. Chandrachud & Justice Sanjiv Khanna & Justice B.R. Gavai
subject: Arbitration Law

summary.background: Parties entered into a commercial subcontract containing an arbitration clause. The contract was insufficiently stamped under State Stamp Act. When dispute arose, petitioner sought urgent interim protection under Section 9 to prevent bank guarantee invocation.
summary.issues: Whether non-stamping or insufficient stamping of a commercial contract bars courts from entertaining applications for urgent interim relief under Section 9 of Arbitration Act.
summary.relevantLaw: Arbitration & Conciliation Act 1996 — Section 9 & Indian Stamp Act 1899 — Section 35.
summary.courtReasoning: Following the 7-Judge Constitution Bench principles in NN Global II, the Court reaffirmed that defect of stamping is a curable procedural irregularity. Section 9 court can grant urgent interim protection while impounding the document for stamp duty adjudication.
summary.holding: Unstamped or insufficiently stamped agreement does not prevent courts from granting urgent Section 9 interim measures.
summary.keyPrinciple: Interim protection under Section 9 cannot be stalled due to stamp impounding delays.
summary.outcome: Appeal allowed; High Court order denying interim protection set aside; interim injunction granted.
